content: Shock is a frequently encountered condition in the Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU), and its management requires careful consideration. It is essential to identify the type of shock, as treatment strategies differ depending on the underlying cause. Norepinephrine is a reliable first-line vasopressor for most types of shock, and fluid resuscitation is a critical initial step in managing all types of shock except cardiogenic shock. Norepinephrine Mechanism of Action: Norepinephrine acts on both alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, causing vasoconstriction of blood vessels, and beta-1 adrenergic receptors, which increase cardiac output. Indications: Septic shock Cardiogenic shock It is preferred over dopamine in cardiogenic shock due to a lower risk of tachyarrhythmias. In cases where the type of shock is unclear, norepinephrine can be used as a first-line agent. Dosing: 1–30 mcg/min. Dopamine Mechanism of Action: Dopamine acts on alpha-1 (vasoconstriction), beta-1 (increased cardiac output), and dopamine receptors (distributed throughout the body). Its effects are dose-dependent: At low doses (1–10 mcg/min), it primarily acts on cardiac receptors with minimal vasoconstriction. At higher doses, it exerts both vasoconstrictive and cardiac effects. Indications: Cardiogenic shock Septic shock (as a second-line treatment) Side Effects: Dopamine is arrhythmogenic and should be avoided in patients prone to arrhythmias. Dosing: 1–20 mcg/min. Vasopressin Mechanism of Action: Vasopressin stimulates V1 receptors in vascular and gastrointestinal smooth muscles, leading to vasoconstriction. It also has an anti-diuretic effect. Indications: Septic shock (as a second-line treatment) Side Effects: Vasopressin can cause coronary and splanchnic vasoconstriction. It should be avoided in patients with NSTEMI (non-ST elevation myocardial infarction) or gut ischemia. It may be used cautiously in cases of mild troponin elevation but should be avoided if troponin levels are significantly elevated (e.g., >5–10). Dosing: 0.03 units/min (this is the only vasopressor that is not titrated). Phenylephrine Mechanism of Action: Phenylephrine acts exclusively on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, causing vasoconstriction. It has no effect on cardiac receptors and is considered cardiac neutral. Indications: Neurogenic shock Thirdor fourth-line vasopressor in septic shock (used when refractory to norepinephrine, dopamine, and vasopressin) Side Effects: Phenylephrine can cause reflex bradycardia but does not induce tachycardia. Dosing: 20–300 mcg/min. Dobutamine Mechanism of Action: Dobutamine acts on beta-1 adrenergic receptors (increasing cardiac output) and beta-2 adrenergic receptors (causing vasodilation). While it enhances cardiac output, it also increases the risk of hypotension due to its vasodilatory effects. Indications: Cardiogenic shock Low-output septic shock Side Effects: Tachyarrhythmias (due to beta-1 effects) Hypotension (due to beta-2 effects) In cases of hypotension caused by dobutamine, an additional vasopressor with alpha-adrenergic effects (e.g., norepinephrine or dopamine) should be added to counteract the hypotensive effects.
